content: Birth weight refers to the weight of a newborn at the time of delivery. It is closely associated with the gestational age at which the baby is born. During pregnancy, birth weight can be estimated by measuring the fundal height of the uterus. A baby whose weight falls within the normal range for its gestational age is classified as appropriate for gestational age (AGA). Conversely, babies whose weight is either above or below this range are considered to have experienced an atypical rate of development, which may indicate complications during pregnancy that could affect either the baby or the mother. Several factors influence whether a baby’s birth weight falls outside the AGA range. These include genetic predispositions, the mother’s health status during pregnancy, environmental influences, and other factors such as multiple births. In cases of multiple births, it is common for one or more babies to fall outside the AGA range, with one baby often being more affected than the other(s). Numerous studies have explored potential associations between birth weight and various health outcomes later in life. These include conditions such as diabetes, obesity, tobacco use, and even intelligence. Conditions Associated with Birth Weight Babies may be classified as either large for gestational age (LGA) or small for gestational age (SGA) if their birth weight deviates significantly from the expected range for their gestational age. Influence of Birth Weight on Adult Life Research has investigated how birth weight may impact an individual’s health and development in adulthood. Specific areas of interest include obesity, diabetes, and intelligence. Obesity Babies born at either extreme of the birth weight spectrum—whether small for gestational age (SGA) or large for gestational age (LGA)—are believed to have an elevated risk of developing obesity later in life. Diabetes Low birth weight has been associated with an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes in adulthood. Intelligence Some studies suggest a positive correlation between higher birth weight and higher intelligence quotient (IQ), indicating that increased birth weight may be linked to improved cognitive outcomes. Effects of Birth Weight on the Mother There is evidence to suggest that a child’s birth weight may have implications for the mother’s long-term health. Specifically, higher or lower birth weights in offspring have been linked to an increased risk of cardiovascular disease in the mother.
